synthesis.headline: Arizona supercells and Four Corners flooding as Josephine goes extratropical and Vance heads for major hurricane
synthesis.narrative:
For a second day, the Western trough is the story. Supercells kept going overnight in east-central Arizona under Severe Thunderstorm Watches 691 and 692. SPC has a Slight risk across central and eastern Arizona into western New Mexico, with storms strengthening over the high terrain between 18 and 21Z. Expect large hail, including isolated stones of 2 inches or more, a few tornadoes in east-central Arizona, and damaging winds as storms cluster into New Mexico. Tropical moisture is driving flash flooding: WPC has a Moderate risk over the high terrain of southern Utah and Colorado and a Slight risk across the Four Corners. Heavy snow is possible in the southern Sierra and Colorado Rockies. Off the East Coast, Subtropical Storm Josephine (55 kt, 988 mb, about 195 miles south-southeast of Nantucket) should become extratropical today. It is forecast to peak near 70 kt early Friday as it passes well south of Newfoundland, bringing gale gusts to the Northeast coast, Mid-Atlantic coastal flooding and dangerous surf as far as Atlantic Canada. In the eastern Pacific, Tropical Storm Vance (45 kt) could intensify rapidly to a peak near 105 kt Saturday.

At 500 mb the pattern is amplified and slow-moving. A Pacific coast trough is moving inland over the Great Basin, ridging peaks near 588-590 dam over northern Mexico and the southern Plains, and an open trough sits over the Great Lakes and Northeast (570-575 dam). A 65-70 kt jet streak off Baja gives 40-50+ kt of deep-layer shear over upper-60s dewpoints near Phoenix, a lot of moisture for late October. The downstream ridge brings well-above-normal warmth and possible record-warm lows to the Plains and Upper Midwest. The eastern trough is the one Josephine is interacting with, and it leaves the East clear and cold, with frost or freeze through the weekend. Vance's steering weakens after day 3, so its track guidance spreads widely.

On Friday the lead shortwave ejects into the northern Plains while a cutoff low lags across the Desert Southwest. SPC has a Marginal risk in New Mexico (supercells, a tornado possible), and WPC has a Slight flood risk there. Sunday brings 1-2 inches of rain from the Texas Panhandle to Nebraska. After that the trough flattens, a closed low crosses the Pacific Northwest on Monday, and the flow turns quasi-zonal by Thursday. Florida's east coast could see a few inches of rain by Tuesday. The Western trough regime, in place since the 19th, breaks up for now. But both the 6-10 and 8-14 day charts keep a negative anomaly of about 9 dam off California and Baja beneath a northeast Pacific–Alaska ridge, so the troughing reloads offshore rather than disappearing.
synthesis.climate_context: This is a very strong El Niño. The Oceanic Niño Index reached +2.16 for July-September, up from -0.39 last winter, though the pace of warming has slowed slightly; the table has no as-of date, so check it against CPC's latest update. The current weather is consistent with typical El Niño patterns. A vigorous subtropical jet is feeding moisture and shear into the Southwest, and the eastern Pacific remains active, with Vance expected to reach major-hurricane strength in late October. In the Atlantic, upper-level winds are expected to stop the trough east-southeast of Bermuda from developing, which also fits the pattern, though a single case doesn't prove the link. Teleconnection indices are stale and were left out.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC Mesoscale Discussion 2396 (valid to 1445Z) covers the Mogollon Rim from east of Phoenix to Show Low, with peak estimates of 1.5-2.5 inch hail and possible tornadoes of 85-110 mph. Isolated severe storms are possible in the Great Basin, and a cluster may cross from northern Nevada into southern Idaho. In Canada, a 986 hPa low west of Hudson Bay is pushing a cold front toward the Great Lakes. In Mexico, swells from Vance reach the southern and southwestern coasts this weekend.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This 0900Z analysis for Thursday, October 22, 2026 is dominated by a deep marine cyclone well off the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast coast, labeled Subtropical Storm Josephine, with a central pressure near 996 mb and a boxed max wind of 55 kt gusting to 65 kt. That system produces the tightest isobar packing on the chart, along the western Atlantic periphery, while the continental interior is comparatively slack, with weak highs near 1024-1025 mb over the Ohio Valley/Mid-Mississippi region and Great Lakes, and another near 1023-1025 mb over the central Rockies/Plains. Those highs are modest and mainly mark cool, settled air rather than driving the weather on their own.

The most active frontal zone runs across the northern tier: a cold front with a wavy boundary from the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies eastward toward the Upper Midwest, with embedded lows near 1009-1013 mb over the northern Plains and along the Canadian border. A stationary or warm-front segment is drawn near the Great Lakes, and a quasi-stationary boundary stretches across the southern Plains toward the Gulf Coast. Along the Pacific coast, several weak lows (about 1006-1009 mb) and an occluded or cold frontal structure off Washington and Oregon bring a Pacific system toward the coast, while a trough sits over the Great Basin and California.

Gradient is tight over the western Atlantic near Josephine and moderately firm along the northern frontal zone, but slack across the central and eastern U.S. under the weak highs. Moisture and lift appear focused along the northern cold front from the Dakotas toward the Great Lakes, along the Pacific Northwest coast ahead of the incoming front, and offshore Florida and the Southeast coast, where the dewpoints in the 60s and 70s sit near the storm's western flank. The surface chart only marks where boundaries sit; the actual lift depends on upper-level support not shown here.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
This CMC surface analysis, valid 00Z Thursday 22 October 2026, is a polar-projection chart, so the upper half is high Arctic and the Canadian Archipelago, with the Canadian provinces and the contiguous US confined to the lower center. The dominant Canadian-sector feature is a 1037 hPa high near the center of the frame, which by the visible coastlines appears to sit over the Arctic islands or adjacent Arctic ocean well north of the mainland. It is flanked by lows of 998 and 1013 hPa and by 981 and 986 hPa centers on either side, giving a tight gradient on its east and west flanks where the closely packed isobars are most evident.

Across the mainland, the 986 hPa low just west of Hudson Bay (position approximate, since the bay's outline is hard to separate from the clutter of station plots) trails a cold front southeast and then south-southwest toward the Great Lakes region. A second front arcs from the Quebec and Labrador side down the east coast, ahead of which a broad trough with a 1000 hPa low sits north of the lakes. Together these boundaries sweep the eastern half of the continent, with highs of 1024 to 1029 hPa behind them over the Great Lakes and northeastern US and a ridge near 1025 hPa over the central Plains.

Off the Atlantic Canadian seaboard, a 994 hPa low is labeled as sub-tropical storm Josephine near 37.6N 69.3W, well south of Nova Scotia, with a strong high (1029 hPa) to its north and a front wrapping its western flank. Farther north, a 981 hPa low and a 994 hPa low near Baffin Island and Davis Strait are plausible by their placement relative to Greenland's coast, though I am less certain of their exact geography.

On the Pacific side, a deep 965 hPa low dominates the far northwest of the frame, with a multi-barbed front system. By the visible geography it appears to sit over the Bering Sea and Alaska area, well outside Canada, with a weaker 1003 hPa low and its front lying off the Pacific coast.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 500 mb pattern is a high-amplitude longwave with a trough over the Pacific coast and western Canada and a broad ridge axis running from the Desert Southwest and Rockies north-northeastward toward the Canadian Prairies. Contours are labeled in decameters as four digits on the chart (e.g. 5760), which equals 576 dam; the ridge crest reaches roughly 588-590 dam over northern Mexico and the southern Plains, where the blue H sits, and 576-580 dam extends well north into the northern Plains. Over the Gulf Coast and Southeast the heights remain high (about 583-592 dam), with a weaker trough axis in the Great Lakes and Northeast, where heights drop to roughly 570-575 dam.

The strongest jet streak is the shaded maximum off southern California and Baja, with winds exceeding about 65-70 kt in the yellow core, oriented northwest to southeast on the western flank of the ridge before curving anticyclonically. A second, weaker band of strong flow appears over the Gulf of Alaska and the Pacific Northwest, with another maximum in the upper right near the Canadian Maritimes and the North Atlantic. The strong gradient along the Pacific coast implies the jet axis hugging the ridge's upstream side.

I see no closed low over the lower 48. The troughing in the Northeast and Great Lakes is open and appears broadly neutral to slightly positively tilted, with the 570-575 dam contours running southwest-northeast. In the Pacific Northwest and southwestern Canada, the northwest-oriented contours suggest a shortwave trough descending toward the ridge.

The flow looks quasi-stationary and amplified rather than progressive: a western ridge with eastern troughing, but no high-over-low couplet, so this is not a Rex block. It reads as a ridge-trough pair with the strongest jet kinking around the western ridge crest.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most organized feature is a comma-shaped cloud mass off the New England and Gulf of Maine coast, with its white cloud shield wrapped around a cyclonic center near the Maine/Nova Scotia offshore waters. A broad orange-brown dry band curls around its southern and southwestern flank, running southeast from the Mid-Atlantic coast out over the western Atlantic, consistent with dry air wrapping around the cyclone's base. Over the interior East the air mass is largely uniform olive-green, a muted field with no sharp dry streamers, so there is little to point to there in the way of strong upper-level forcing.

In the West, the saturated reds, magentas and purples along the Pacific Northwest and northern California coast mark a deep, cold, dry upper-level environment on the cyclonic side of a trough, with the edge of the purple/blue field offshore suggesting the likely jet corridor along the trough's eastern side. Cloud bands extend from there southeast across the Great Basin, Rockies and into the southern High Plains, with a brighter white convective-looking cluster near the Colorado/New Mexico area, though the exact state placement is uncertain at this projection. That cloud axis, running from the Pacific Northwest down toward northern Mexico and the Texas Big Bend region, is the best candidate for the trough's moist axis.

Across the Gulf of Mexico, the broad orange-brown area is dry mid- and upper-tropospheric air consistent with ridging, not a stratospheric intrusion, since it sits in anticyclonic flow with no sharp edges. A darker green swath from southern Mexico and the Yucatan northward marks a moist tropical corridor, while scattered cloud over the Bahamas, Cuba and the Greater Antilles, and a bright cluster in the Caribbean in the lower right, show tropical convection without clear organized rotation.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary:
The most organized tropical feature is a compact, bright white cloud shield with curved banding in the eastern Pacific, roughly 10 to 15 degrees west of the Mexican Pacific coast and well south of Baja California, with a smaller convective cluster to its west. The curved structure suggests a tropical cyclone or developing system, but the airmass product cannot confirm intensity or classification. Across the Caribbean, scattered convective clusters sit north of Venezuela and over the central basin, with another disorganized area near the Panama and Costa Rica coast. The Gulf of Mexico and western Atlantic are dominated by broad green moist tropical air with orange-brown dry patches over the Gulf, which fits drier mid- to upper-level air there rather than any stratospheric intrusion.

Over the northern Atlantic, a well-defined cloud band extends from the Canadian Maritimes and the waters off the Northeast US toward the east and southeast, with a cluster of bright convective cloud in the central subtropical Atlantic. The implied polar jet corridor runs along the sharp transition from green to orange-brown to purple-blue air north and east of that cloud band, with a pronounced swirl of deep blue and purple near the right limb off southeastern Greenland or the northern Atlantic that points to a deep cold-core trough. Dark blue and purple dominate the high-latitude edges of the disk, consistent with cold, dry upper-tropospheric air, though the extreme viewing angle there distorts both geography and color, so Arctic boundaries should be read cautiously.

Across Canada the northern edge shows alternating orange and blue-purple bands, suggesting a meandering airmass boundary, but the limb geometry limits how precisely trough and ridge axes can be placed. In the Southern Hemisphere, a large comma-shaped cloud mass over southeastern Brazil and the adjacent South Atlantic indicates a frontal system with a distinct dry intrusion behind it, visible as orange and red tones in the far south Pacific and off Patagonia.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary:
This CPC outlook for October 27-31, 2026 (issued October 21) favors above-normal temperatures across most of the country. The strongest lower-48 signal, the 50-60% category, covers a broad swath from Texas and Oklahoma northeast through the Lower Mississippi and Tennessee Valleys, the Midwest and Great Lakes, and into Ohio, Kentucky and West Virginia. Probabilities relax to 40-50% over the central Plains, much of the Southwest and Southeast coast, Minnesota and the Mid-Atlantic, and to 33-40% (leaning above) over the interior West, northern Plains and parts of northern New England. Alaska carries the highest confidence on the chart, with 70-80% across most of the state and an 80-90% core over the western mainland. Hawaii leans or is likely above, mostly in the 40-60% range.

Below-normal odds are confined to the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, with a 33-40% leaning-below area over Washington, Oregon, northern Idaho and western Montana, and a small 40-50% core near the Montana-Canada border. Near-normal, the gray shading, runs from California and Nevada through the central Rockies toward the northern High Plains, and again over Maine and adjacent northern New England.

Remember that these are probabilities of terciles, not temperature departures, so even the 50-60% area means odds modestly tilted toward warmth rather than a forecast of extreme heat.

On the regime question, the chart alone cannot show the upper-level pattern, so this is inference. The geometry is consistent with ridging over the central and eastern U.S. and a trough or cool northwesterly flow near the northwest corner of the country, with the warm anomaly axis oriented southwest to northeast and a cooler-to-near-normal zone running along the West Coast and northern tier. That reads as a persistent western-trough, eastern-ridge configuration through the end of the month. Nothing here signals a breakdown, though the weak 33-50% values across the interior West and the near-normal band suggest lower confidence at the pattern's transition zone, where a shift in trough position would change the outcome first.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly prognostic, valid Oct 27-31, 2026, with solid green height contours (labeled 5220 to 5880, i.e. 522 to 588 dam) and dashed anomaly lines at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. The anomaly labels (30, 90, 150, 210, 270) are in meters, so the largest positive center is about 270+ m, or roughly 27 dam, and the dashed-line spacing of 6 dam is steady and checks out. The strongest positive anomaly sits over the northeast Pacific and Gulf of Alaska, labeled near 210-270 m, with a broad positive tongue extending northeast across Alaska and the Yukon. A second positive center of about 150 m (15 dam) lies over the Arctic Ocean north of Alaska and the Beaufort Sea region, linking to the Pacific ridging.

The main negative center is over northeastern Canada and Greenland, with the 5220 contour closing off a deep low there and anomalies around -150 m (about -15 dam). A separate negative center of roughly -90 m (about -9 dam) lies off the Pacific Northwest and California coast, with blue dashed contours also reaching into the Northwest and northern Great Basin. A weaker positive area, labeled near 30-90 m, covers the eastern Midwest, Ohio Valley and Southeast.

The implied ridge axis runs from the northeast Pacific northward through Alaska, so the western ridge is displaced well to the north and west rather than sitting over the western U.S. The trough axes are off the West Coast and over northeastern Canada. The zero-anomaly line (purple) bends over the Pacific Northwest and Rockies, so negative departures cover the Northwest and part of the northern Rockies while the southern and eastern U.S. sit on the positive side.

Positive anomalies over western North America are therefore concentrated at high latitude, over Alaska and the Yukon, rather than over the contiguous western states. The strong height gradient between the Gulf of Alaska high and the offshore trough suggests meridional rather than zonal flow, though the 5640-5760 contours lying roughly west-east across the central U.S. imply fairly zonal flow south of 40N. A single ensemble-mean chart cannot show trend, so whether the ridge is retreating or amplifying cannot be determined from this panel alone.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is the CPC 8-14 day 500 mb heights and anomalies chart, made 21 Oct 2026 and valid Oct 29 to Nov 4. Contours are labeled in meters (5220 to 5820 m, i.e. roughly 522 to 582 dam), with dashed anomaly lines at 60 m (6 dam) intervals. The anomaly labels on the chart (30, 90, -30, -90) are in meters, so the strongest centers are about 9 dam, not 90 dam.

The dominant feature is a deep, broad trough over the Arctic and northeastern Canada. A closed height contour near 5220 to 5280 m sits over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and northern Baffin Island/Greenland, with the tight contour packing wrapping around it from the Gulf of Alaska across Canada to the Atlantic. The anomaly field only partly matches this: positive anomalies of roughly +30 m (3 dam) flank the trough over northern Canada and the Great Lakes/Northeast, with a weak +30 m center near the eastern Great Lakes and Northeast coast.

Over the Pacific and western North America, the chart shows a strong positive anomaly center of about +90 m (9 dam) over the northeast Pacific south of Alaska, near the left edge of the domain, with positive anomalies extending toward the Alaska coast. A negative center of about -90 m (-9 dam) sits farther south over the eastern Pacific off California and Baja, with the cyan -30 m contour reaching into the Southwest.

On the specific question of positive anomalies over western Canada, the northern Rockies, and the northern Plains: none are plotted there. The red dashed positive contours stay near the Pacific coast of Alaska and northwestern Canada, then turn up toward the Yukon (a +30 m line near 60N), while the northern Rockies and northern Plains lie between the dashed purple/cyan negative lines and the 5400 to 5580 m contours. The ridge core is therefore not over the northern Rockies. It is displaced west over the northeast Pacific, with the implied ridge axis running toward Alaska. Downstream, strongly packed contours imply a northwesterly flow regime from western Canada into the central US, with a trough axis from the Arctic southward toward the central and eastern US. The southern tier of the US sits near the 5760 to 5820 m contours, consistent with a retained but not dominant subtropical ridge.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 1)
sources.summary:
This WPC Day 1 Excessive Rainfall Outlook, valid 12Z Thursday October 22 to 12Z Friday October 23, 2026, shows three categories: Marginal (green, at least 5%), Slight (yellow, at least 15%) and Moderate (red, at least 40%). No High risk (magenta) is drawn. The largest footprint is the Marginal area, spanning much of the interior West from the Great Basin and southern Idaho through Utah and western Colorado, extending south into Arizona and western New Mexico, with an arm reaching toward southern Nevada and southeastern California. Separate small Marginal areas appear along the central California coast and over the southern Florida peninsula and Keys.

A Slight risk is nested inside the broad Marginal area over the Four Corners region, covering eastern Utah, western and central Colorado, and northern New Mexico and Arizona. The only Moderate risk is a small east-west oval in central Colorado, roughly along and west of the Front Range and centered near the middle of the state, which makes it the highest-risk area on the chart. The risk areas are clustered over high terrain and the Continental Divide, which suggests orographic enhancement and slow-moving or repeated downpours over complex topography. The chart cannot confirm the driver, but the placement fits an upper-level disturbance interacting with the mountains, rather than a tropical system. The southern Florida Marginal area is separate and small, and the chart alone does not indicate its source.

sources.title: Excessive Rainfall Outlook (Day 2)
sources.summary:
This Day 2 outlook, valid 12Z Friday Oct 23 through 12Z Saturday Oct 24, 2026, shows two risk categories. A broad Marginal (at least 5%) area covers much of New Mexico, running from roughly the Arizona border eastward toward the central part of the state, and extending south into the far western tip of Texas near El Paso and the adjacent Mexican border. Embedded within it is a small Slight (at least 15%) area, shaded yellow with an orange outline, over south-central New Mexico, in the corridor north of the Texas and Mexico borders.

A separate, thin Marginal line appears off the southeast Florida coast, hugging the Atlantic side of the peninsula from roughly the Palm Beach area southward toward the Keys. It is drawn as a narrow coastal strip, so it likely reflects a risk focused along the immediate shoreline.

No Moderate or High risk is drawn anywhere on the chart. The chart shows risk categories only, not rainfall amounts, and nothing in it indicates how this compares with a Day 1 outlook for the same system.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary:
As of 353 AM EDT Thu Oct 22 2026 (valid through 12Z Sat Oct 24): Subtropical Storm Josephine is moving farther into the Western Atlantic and is likely to become post-tropical today. Brief storm-force gusts (50+ kt) are possible southeast of Nantucket, with inland southern New England gusts of 20-45 mph and possible beach erosion. Conditions improve in the Northeast today.

A deep Western U.S. trough pulls anomalous tropical moisture into California, the Great Basin, and the Four Corners today, with a cold front sparking storms. A moderate excessive rainfall risk (40%+) covers southern Utah into southwest Colorado, and a slight risk (15%+) covers the Four Corners and southern Nevada, with flash flooding in washes, slot canyons, and burn scars. The threat shifts to the Southern and Central High Plains Friday and Saturday.

SPC has a slight risk (2/5) of severe storms over southeast Arizona and southwest New Mexico, with hail and wind. Heavy snow is possible in the southern Sierra and Colorado Rockies today, shifting to the Northern Rockies Friday.

Western temperatures stay below average. Above- to well-above-average temperatures, with possible record minimums, are expected in the Northern/Central Plains and Upper Midwest. The East has clear skies, below-average temperatures, and frost or freeze through the weekend. Florida storms are expected in the south, with possible excessive rainfall by the weekend.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Issued 7:44 AM CDT Thursday, October 22, 2026, valid through 12Z October 23. A slight risk of severe thunderstorms covers central and eastern Arizona into western New Mexico. Occasional supercells have persisted overnight over east-central Arizona, supported by a 50-70 kt mid-level jet, 40-50+ kt deep-layer shear, and 500-1500 J/kg MUCAPE. More intense storms are expected by 18-21Z over the higher terrain as an upper trough moves inland over the Great Basin. Large hail is the primary threat, with isolated 2+ inch hail possible. A few tornadoes are possible in east-central Arizona in the afternoon. Damaging winds increase by mid to late afternoon as convection spreads into western New Mexico and may cluster. The severe threat peaks mid to late afternoon and continues at an isolated level into the evening before weakening eastward into western and central New Mexico. Farther north, isolated severe hail and wind are possible across the Great Basin, with a small cluster possibly spreading from northern Nevada into southern Idaho and producing strong to locally severe gusts. The Marginal Risk for coastal southern California was removed.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary:
SPC Mesoscale Discussion 2396, issued 0740 AM CDT Thu Oct 22 2026 and valid through 1445Z, covers central and eastern Arizona near and south of the Mogollon Rim. It concerns Severe Thunderstorm Watches 691 and 692. Intensifying thunderstorm development remains possible through 7-9 AM MST, including a couple of evolving supercells capable of large hail, locally damaging wind gusts, and at least some tornado risk.

The strongest recent storms have focused near and south of the Mogollon Rim, from east of Phoenix north toward the Show Low vicinity. Objective analysis shows a better instability corridor lingering west and southwest of Flagstaff into the Greater Phoenix area, with surface dew points in the upper 60s F, as an upstream mid-level trough slowly pivots toward the region. Forcing and diurnal heating could support further intensification through 14-16Z, with strong deep-layer shear continuing.

Most probable peak values: tornado intensity 85-110 mph; wind gusts 55-70 mph; hail 1.50-2.50 inches.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
As of 800 AM EDT Thursday, October 22, 2026, the NHC is issuing advisories on Subtropical Storm Josephine, a few hundred miles offshore of the Mid-Atlantic U.S. coast.

A separate trough several hundred miles east-southeast of Bermuda is producing disorganized showers and thunderstorms. It may develop somewhat over the next day or two as it moves slowly north-northeastward, but upper-level winds are expected to become too strong for further development by the weekend. Formation chances are low, 10 percent through both 48 hours and 7 days.

As of 500 AM PDT Thursday, October 22, 2026, the NHC is issuing advisories on Tropical Storm Vance, several hundred miles south-southwest of Acapulco, Mexico.

In the central Pacific, an area of low pressure is expected to form near the International Date Line, a few hundred miles west-southwest of Johnston Atoll, late this weekend or early next week. Conditions appear conducive to gradual development afterward as it moves generally eastward to east-northeastward. Formation chance is near 0 percent through 48 hours and 30 percent through 7 days.

sources.title: NHC Active Storm Advisories
sources.summary:
As of 2026-10-22 09:00 UTC, the National Hurricane Center is tracking two storms.

SUBTROPICAL STORM JOSEPHINE (Atlantic): Max sustained winds 55 kt (65 mph), minimum pressure 988 mb. Center near 38.7N 68.3W, about 195 mi SSE of Nantucket, moving NE at 13 mph and accelerating. Tropical-storm-force winds extend out to 415 mi from the center. Josephine is expected to lose subtropical characteristics today as it moves over cooler water and interacts with an amplifying upper trough. It is forecast to become a hurricane-force extratropical cyclone within 24 hours, peaking near 70 kt (80 mph) around early Friday (23/0600Z), then weaken as it turns east, passing well south of Newfoundland. It is forecast to dissipate by Saturday (26/0600Z). Track guidance is tightly clustered. No coastal watches or warnings are in effect. Hazards: gale-force gusts possible along the northeastern U.S. coast through today (local NWS products apply); minor to locally moderate coastal flooding along the Mid-Atlantic coast through the week around high tide; large swells causing life-threatening surf and rip currents along the eastern U.S. seaboard and Atlantic Canada.

TROPICAL STORM VANCE (eastern Pacific): Max sustained winds 45 kt (50 mph), minimum pressure 1000 mb. Center near 9.7N 101.5W, about 510 mi SSW of Acapulco, moving W at 7 mph, expected to turn NW over the next couple of days. Tropical-storm-force winds extend out to 80 mi. Vance is forecast to strengthen, with rapid intensification possible, to a major hurricane by the weekend. Peak intensity near 105 kt (120 mph) around Saturday (24/1800Z), then gradual weakening. Confidence in track falls markedly after day 3 because of weak steering flow, so there is a wide spread among guidance. Probabilities of rapid intensification were trimmed slightly in the latest model run. No coastal watches or warnings are in effect. Hazard: swells from Vance will reach the coasts of southern and southwestern Mexico this weekend into next week, likely causing life-threatening surf and rip currents.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows a rapid shift from cool to warm conditions across 2026. The three-month running anomaly rose from -0.39 in DJF (December-February) to +0.11 in FMA, crossing the El Niño threshold of +0.5 in MAM (March-May) at +0.46 and reaching +0.95 in AMJ. It continued climbing to +1.39 in MJJ, +1.80 in JJA, and +2.16 in JAS (July-September), the highest value in the table. A JAS value of +2.16 falls in the very strong El Niño range (at least +2.0) under CPC's strength categories. The rate of increase has slowed slightly in recent seasons, from roughly +0.4 to +0.5 per season in spring and early summer to about +0.36 in the most recent step. The table gives no as-of date and does not specify which seasons are observed and which are forecast, so the latest values should be checked against the current official ENSO update before use.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary:
CPC teleconnection indices, as of 2026-09-30. This table is stale: its newest values are 22 days old and CPC has not updated it, so none of these readings should be treated as current.

PNA: latest +0.12, near neutral. The 7-day mean (-0.41) rose from -1.51 the prior week, recovering from a trough near -2.04 earlier in the window.

AO: latest -0.26, near neutral. The 7-day mean (+0.04) fell from +1.73, a drop of 1.69, after strongly positive readings early in the window.

NAO: latest -0.78, the most negative value in the window. The 7-day mean (-0.15) fell from +0.28, so the index is trending negative.

These are observed values, and teleconnection signals are weak in this season, so treat them only as directional support.
